'''Ronald Whittam''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|FRS}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=David J. |last2=Naftalin |first2=Richard J. |date=2025 |title=Ronald Whittam. 21 March 1925—16 August 2023 |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbm.2024.0030 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=78|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2024.0030 |doi-access=free }}</ref> (21 March 1925 – 16 August 2023) was an English research scientist in the field of [[cell physiology]]. He conducted important studies on the mechanism of [[active transport]] of [[ion]]s across animal membranes and its relation to [[cellular metabolism]]. Whittam was the inaugural Chair in Physiology at the [[University of Leicester]], where he was subsequently an [[Emeritus#In academia|Emeritus Professor]].

== Early life and education ==
Ronald Whittam was born in [[Chadderton]], within the [[Metropolitan Borough of Oldham]], [[Lancashire]], on 21 March 1925. He is the eldest of three sons and one daughter of Edward Whittam and May Whittam.<ref name="WHO">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=1 December 2007|title=Whittam, Prof. Ronald|url=https://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/10.1093/ww/9780199540884.001.0001/ww-9780199540884-e-39689|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=29 January 2021|website=WHO'S WHO & WHO WAS WHO|publisher=Oxford University Press|language=En|doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U39689|isbn=978-0-19-954088-4|ref=WHO}}</ref> His parents owned a bakery business in [[Butler Green]], [[Chadderton]].<ref>Washbrook Methodist Church Centenary leaflet, 1962</ref> He left school at the age of 14 to work in the family business. He voluntarily attended educational evening classes and at the age of 16 had day release to the [[Oldham College|Municipal Technical College, Oldham]].  He achieved the School Certificate.<ref name="PSINT">{{Cite journal|last=Miller|first=David J.|date=12 August 2014|title=Oral History Project - transcript of Ronald Whittam|url=https://www.physoc.org/about-us/history-archives/oral-histories/|department=|journal=The Physiological Society - Oral History|location=[[Wellcome Institute]], London, UK|publisher=[[The Physiological Society]]|volume=|pages=|ref=PSINT|via=}}</ref>

Whittam reached the age of 18 during [[World War II]] in 1943 and joined the [[Royal Air Force]]. He was selected to join the PNB scheme: pilot, navigator, bomb-aimer. He passed the PNB scheme, in 50 Initial Training Wing at [[RAF Bridgnorth]], [[Shropshire]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=29 January 2021|title=RAF Bridgnorth personnel 50ITW|url=http://rafbridgnorth.org.uk/dutch/1945_50_itw.html|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=RAFBridgnorth.org.uk}}</ref> In 1947 he was [[Demobilisation of the British Armed Forces after the Second World War|demobbed]] from [[National Service (Armed Forces) Act 1939|National Service]], then commenced university life.<ref name="University of Leicester obit"/>

Whittam received his [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] degree in [[Chemistry]], at the [[University of Manchester]] in 1951.<ref name="WHO" /> His tutor was Thomas K. Walker who by then had finished working with [[Chaim Weizmann]] in the University.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Walker|first=Thomas Kennedy|date=1970|title=Announcements - Obituary|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/2281358c0|journal=Nature|language=English|volume=228|issue=5278|pages=1358–1359|doi=10.1038/2281358c0|issn=1476-4687|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He gained an early insight for research with Professor Herbert Stanley Raper and Alfred Alexander Harper.<ref name="PSINT" />

Whittam founded the Labour Student Club in the Faculty at the University of Manchester and was a member of the executive of the newly formed [[Labour Students|National Association of Labour Students Organisations]],<ref>National Association of Labour Student Organisations archive, Labour History Archive and Study Centre, Manchester, UK. National Archives Ref: LP/GS/NALSO</ref> along with [[Fred Jarvis]], [[Dick Mabon]] and [[Bill Wedderburn]].<ref name="PSINT" />

== Career and research ==
In 1951 Whittam was selected by Professor Sir [[Hans Krebs (biochemist)|Hans Krebs]] to conduct research in the [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]] unit - Department of [[Biochemistry]], [[University of Sheffield]]. He resided in Stephenson Hall where he met another biochemist: [[Gregorio Weber]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Whittam|first=Ron|date=|title=A friend and mentor Gregorio Weber|url=https://g-weber.wixsite.com/tributes/a-friend-and-mentor-by-ron-whittam|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=1 February 2021|website=|language=en}}</ref> He received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]]. His external examiner was Professor Sir [[Alan Hodgkin]]. He continued research upon being awarded a John Stokes Fellowship till 1955.<ref name="WHO" /> He published several papers, including with Bob Davies,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=WHITTAM|first1=R.|last2=DAVIES|first2=R. E.|date=1954|title=Energy Requirements for Ion Transport in Steady-State Systems|journal=Nature|volume=173|issue=4402|pages=494|doi=10.1038/173494a0|pmid=13144792|bibcode=1954Natur.173..494W|s2cid=4178441|issn=0028-0836|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Whittam|first1=R.|last2=Davies|first2=R. E.|date=1 March 1954|title=Relations between metabolism and the rate of turnover of sodium and potassium in guinea pig kidney-cortex slices|url= |journal=Biochemical Journal|volume=56|issue=3|pages=445–453|doi=10.1042/bj0560445|pmid=13140226|pmc=1269645|issn=0306-3283}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Whittam|first1=R.|last2=Davies|first2=R. E.|date=1 December 1953|title=Active transport of water, sodium, potassium and α-oxoglutarate by kidney-cortex slices|url= |journal=Biochemical Journal|volume=55|issue=5|pages=880–888|doi=10.1042/bj0550880|pmid=13115390|pmc=1269551|issn=0306-3283}}</ref> Hans Breuer,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Breuer|first1=H. J.|last2=Whittam|first2=R.|date=23 January 1957|title=Ion movements in seminal vesicle mucosa|url= |journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=135|issue=1|pages=213–225|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1957.sp005705|pmid=13398976|pmc=1358923|issn=0022-3751}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=|first=|date=1958|title=Potassium transport in seminal vesicle mucosa|journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=143|issue=3|pages=|doi=10.1111/tjp.1958.143.issue-3|issn=0022-3751|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[Hans Krebs (biochemist)|Professor Sir Hans Krebs]]  and Reg Hems.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=May 1957|title=Potassium uptake of ''Alcaligenes faecalis''|url=https://portlandpress.com/biochemj/article/66/1/53/50298/Potassium-uptake-of-Alcaligenes-faecalis|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=29 January 2021|journal=Biochemical Journal|volume=66|issue=1|pages=55–60|doi=10.1042/bj0660053|last1=Krebs|first1=H. A.|last2=Whittam|first2=R.|last3=Hems|first3=R.|pmid=13426108|pmc=1199964}}</ref>

Later in 1955, Whittam became a [[Beit Memorial Fellowships for Medical Research|Beit Memorial Fellow]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] in the Department of Physiology. He conducted research there and was among eminent physiologist in the department, including Lord [[Edgar Adrian]], Professor Sir [[Alan Hodgkin]], Professor Sir [[Bryan Matthews]], [[Joseph Needham]] and [[Gilbert Smithson Adair|Gilbert Adair]].<ref name="PSINT" /> Whittam and Matthews were both members of [[King's College, Cambridge|Kings’ College]]. His Doctoral advisor was [[Richard Keynes]]. He was awarded another [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]].<ref name="WHO" /> Whittam's research was on [[electrolyte]] and water in relation to [[metabolism]]; oxidative [[phosphorylation]]; the relationship between ion transporting water and respiration and [[glycolysis]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=|first=|date=1 February 1960|title=Glycolysis an potassium transport|journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=150|issue=2|pages=|doi=10.1111/tjp.1960.150.issue-2|issn=0022-3751|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Whittam 358–369">{{Cite journal|last=Whittam|first=R.|date=1 September 1960|title=Sodium and potassium movements in kidney cortex slices from newborn animals|url= |journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=153|issue=2|pages=358–369|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1960.sp006539|pmid=13784940|pmc=1359753|issn=0022-3751}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Whittam|first=R.|date=1 December 1960|title=The support of active potassium transport in human red cells by nucleosides and deoxynucleosides|url= |journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=154|issue=3|pages=608–613|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1960.sp006600|pmid=13784942|pmc=1359824|issn=0022-3751}}</ref><ref name="Whittam 614–623">{{Cite journal|last=Whittam|first=R.|date=1 December 1960|title=The high permeability of human red cells to adenine and hypoxanthine and their ribosides|url= |journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=154|issue=3|pages=614–623|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1960.sp006601|pmid=13784941|pmc=1359825|issn=0022-3751}}</ref> He worked with [[Daniel C. Tosteson]] whereby they discovered the making of red cell ghosts.<ref name="PSINT" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Whittam|first1=Ronald|last2=Tosteson|first2=Daniel C|last3=Hoffman|first3=JF|date=1960|title=Retention of potassium by human erythrocyte ghosts|url=|journal=Nature|volume=185|issue=|pages=186–7|doi=10.1080/19447016008664424|pmid=14402408|issn=1944-7019}}</ref>

[[File:Ronald Whittam in his office at the Department of Physiology University of Leicester.jpg|thumb|Ronald Whittam in his office]]From 1958 to 1966, Whittam was at the [[University of Oxford]]. During that time, he was again in the same department of Sir [[Hans Krebs (biochemist)|Hans Krebs]] who was [[Whitley Professor of Biochemistry]]. He was awarded a [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] at the [[University of Oxford]].  In the first two years he conducted research as scientific research staff of the Medical Research Unit.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Whittam|first1=R.|last2=Guinnebault|first2=M.|date=1 July 1960|title=The Efflux of Potassium from Electroplaques of Electric Eels|url= |journal=Journal of General Physiology|volume=43|issue=6|pages=1171–1191|doi=10.1085/jgp.43.6.1171|pmid=13784938|pmc=2195067|issn=1540-7748}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Whittam|first1=R.|last2=Guinnebault|first2=M.|date=1960|title=The effect of blocking electrical activity on the efflux of potassium from electroplax|journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0006-3002(60)91456-6|volume=45|pages=336–347|doi=10.1016/0006-3002(60)91456-6|pmid=13784937|issn=0006-3002|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="Whittam 358–369" /><ref name="Whittam 614–623" /> Whittam proved the pacemaker effect of the [[Na+/K+-ATPase|sodium pump]] on metabolism with red blood cells.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=WHITTAM|first=Ronald|date=1961|title=Active Cation Transport as a Pace-maker of Respiration|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/191603a0|journal=Nature|volume=191|issue=4788|pages=603–604|doi=10.1038/191603a0|pmid=13784939|bibcode=1961Natur.191..603W|s2cid=4215988|issn=0028-0836|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He spent over half of 1958 at [[Columbia University]], [[New York City|New York]], working with [[David Nachmansohn]] on electrophysiology with single cell electroplaques and the [[electric eel]].<ref name="PSINT" /> Whittam discovered how much potassium is released from a cell of a mammalian.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1 April 1962|title=Proceedings of The Biochemical Society|url= |journal=Biochemical Journal|volume=83|issue=1|pages=1P–15P|doi=10.1042/bj0830001p|pmid=16748946|pmc=1243532|issn=0006-2936}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=1 July 1962|title=Proceedings of The Biochemical Society|url= |journal=Biochemical Journal|volume=84|issue=1|pages=1P–42P|doi=10.1042/bj0840001p|pmid=16748953|pmc=1243645|issn=0006-2936}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=WHITTAM|first=R.|date=1962|title=Directional Effects of Alkali Metal Ions on Adenosine Triphosphate Hydrolysis in Erythrocyte Ghosts|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/196134a0|journal=Nature|volume=196|issue=4850|pages=134–136|doi=10.1038/196134a0|pmid=14000419|bibcode=1962Natur.196..134W|s2cid=27713362|issn=0028-0836|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  In 1960 he became a [[Lecturer]] in the Department of [[Biochemistry]], [[University of Oxford]], joining [[New College, Oxford|New College]], yet also made a member of the [[Common room (university)|Senior Common Room]] at [[Hertford College, Oxford|Hertford College]].<ref name="WHO" /> He was a moderator for exams in [[physiology]] having been asked by [[George Lindor Brown|Professor Sir Lindor Brown]], the [[Waynflete Professorships|Waynflete Professors of Physiology]].<ref name="PSINT" /> A real advance in physiology was made by Whittam in 1962 when he had three Papers published: Spatial asymmetry in the stimulation of a membrane [[ATPase|adenosine triphosphatases]]; the asymmetrical stimulation of a membrane adenosine triphosphatase in relation to active cation transport and directional effects of the alkali metal ions on adenosine triphosphate hydrolysis in erythrocyte ghosts. This research was referred to by The Royal Society upon Whittam being elected a Fellow, "Ronald Whittam conducted important studies of the mechanism of active transport of ions in animal tissues. He demonstrated the special asymmetry of the ATPase of the red blood cell membrane, which acts only when Na<sup>+</sup> is inside and K<sup>+</sup> is outside the membrane. He was the first to demonstrate that active transport can exert a feedback control over the rate of cellular metabolism.  These concepts, of directionality as an inherent part of an enzyme reaction in membranes, are of fundamental significance for the understanding of the relations between physiological function and the mechanism of enzyme action."<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Whittam|first=Ronald|year=1973|title=Royal Society notes|url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/pdf/10.1098/rsnr.1973.0011|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=29 January 2021|journal=Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London|volume=28|doi=10.1098/rsnr.1973.0011|s2cid=202574920|url-access=subscription}}<br>{{Cite web|publisher=The Royal Society |title= Ronald Whittam biography|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/ronald-whittam-12522/|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=29 January 2021|website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>

During 1965, he became a Bruno Mendel [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] conducting research at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]], Israel. There he worked with [[Isidore Edelman|Izzy Edelman]]. [[Ephraim Katzir]] had oversight as Head of the Department of [[Biophysics]].<ref name="WHO" />

In 1966, Whittam became the first Chair of General Physiology in the [[University of Leicester]],<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=University of Leicester|date=|title=Brief History of Department of Molecular and Cell Biology|url=https://le.ac.uk/mcb/about/history|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=29 January 2021|website=le.ac.uk}}</ref> where he established a new Laboratory of Physiology,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=WHITTAM|first=R.|date=1968|title=Control of Membrane Permeability to Potassium in Red Blood Cells|journal=Nature|volume=219|issue=5154|pages=610|doi=10.1038/219610a0|pmid=5665710|bibcode=1968Natur.219..610W|s2cid=8913758|issn=0028-0836|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Priestland|first1=R. N.|last2=Whittam|first2=R.|date=1 September 1968|title=The influence of external sodium ions on the sodium pump in erythrocytes|url= |journal=Biochemical Journal|volume=109|issue=3|pages=369–374|doi=10.1042/bj1090369|pmid=4234831|pmc=1186831|issn=0306-3283}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Whittam|first=R.|date=1 August 1968|title=The incorporation of phosphate into ATP associated with ionic raduation|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/tjp.1968.197.issue-3|journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=197|issue=3|pages=|doi=10.1111/tjp.1968.197.issue-3|issn=0022-3751|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wheeler|first1=K. P.|last2=Whittam|first2=R.|date=1 April 1970|title=The involvement of phosphatidylserine in adenosine triphosphatase activity of the sodium pump|url= |journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=207|issue=2|pages=303–328|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1970.sp009063|pmid=4250771|pmc=1348708|issn=0022-3751}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=|first=|date=1 November 1975|title=The stimulation of phosphate of ouabain binding to the sodium pump...|journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=252|issue=2|pages=|doi=10.1111/tjp.1975.252.issue-2|issn=0022-3751|doi-access=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brand|first1=S C|last2=Whittam|first2=R|date=1 March 1984|title=The effect of furosemide on sodium movements in human red blood cells.|url= |journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=348|issue=1|pages=301–306|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1984.sp015111|pmid=6716288|pmc=1199403|issn=0022-3751}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cotterrell|first1=D.|last2=Whittam|first2=R.|date=1 May 1971|title=The influence of the chloride gradient across red cell membranes on sodium and potassium movements|url= |journal=The Journal of Physiology|volume=214|issue=3|pages=509–536|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1971.sp009446|pmid=4996368|pmc=1331852|issn=0022-3751}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chipperfield|first1=A. R.|last2=Whittam|first2=R.|date=1973|title=Ouabain Binding to the Sodium Pump|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/242062a0|journal=Nature|volume=242|issue=5392|pages=62–63|doi=10.1038/242062a0|pmid=4266529|bibcode=1973Natur.242...62C|s2cid=4212452|issn=0028-0836|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> that was re-titled in 1968 as the [[Academic department|Department]] of Physiology. It was the first Chair of General Physiology to have been created in Britain since Professor Sir [[William Bayliss]] was created Chair at [[University College London]]. He ran one of the largest physiology departments in UK universities, outside of Oxford and Cambridge. A lot of funding was hypothecated from the [[University Grants Committee (United Kingdom)|University Grants Committee]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name="PSINT" />

Whittam made significant contributions to the administration of physiology and the shape of biological sciences in the following positions: 1963 to 1967, member of the Editorial Board of [[Biochemical Journal]]; 1969 to 1974, Honorary Secretary of [[The Physiological Society]]; 1969 to 1974, member of the Biological Research Board of [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]]; 1973 to 1974, Co-Chairman of the Biological Research Board of the [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]], with [[Rodney Robert Porter|Professor Rodney Porter]]; 1974 to 1977, Chairman of the Biological Education Committee of the [[Royal Society]] and [[Institute of Biology]]; 1974 to 1982, member of the Biological Sciences Committee of the [[University Grants Committee (United Kingdom)|University Grants Committee]] 1979 to 1982, Dean of Faculty of Science at the [[University of Leicester]]; 1979 to 1983, member of the Education Committee of the [[Royal Society]].<ref name="WHO" />

In 1983, Whittam became an [[Emeritus#In academia|Emeritus Professor]] of the [[University of Leicester]].<ref name="WHO" /><ref name="PSINT" />

== Personal life and death ==
Whittam married Christine Patricia Margaret Lamb, the second daughter of Canon John W. Lamb, which marriage was officiated by Archbishop [[Michael Ramsey]] in 1957.<ref>{{Cite web|title=History of The Priory {{!}} Bridlington Priory|url=https://bridlingtonpriory.co.uk/history-of-bridlington-priory/|access-date=29 January 2021|language=en-GB}}</ref> They had one son and one daughter.<ref name="WHO" />

Early in his academic career, Whittam was a member of the [[University of Manchester|Manchester University Mountaineering Club]].<ref name="PSINT" /> A passion for walking continued into his nineties.<ref name="WHO" />

Ronald Whittam died at [[Leicester Royal Infirmary]] on 16 August 2023, at the age of 98.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eminent scientist born and raised at Butler Green in Chadderton dies aged 98 |url=https://www.oldham-chronicle.co.uk/news-features/139/main-news/153010/eminent-scientist-born-and-raised-at-butler-green-in-chadderton-dies-aged-98 |access-date=19 August 2023 |website=www.oldham-chronicle.co.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Emeritus Professor Ron Whittam FRS |url=https://le.ac.uk/about/history/obituaries/2023/ron-whittam |access-date=19 August 2023 |website=le.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref>
